title: MOBO-CAPS: Multi-objective Bayesian Optimization with Cardinality-Aware Pareto Selection
claim: The point with the highest standard acquisition score is not the best choice when a fixed-size set must be selected, because replacement-aware scoring picks a different point.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, shared color coding linking function, acquisition, and objective-space views
description: Three side-by-side line and scatter plots on a toy bi-objective problem. Panel (a), 'Objective Functions', shows two smooth curves, f1 in blue and f2 in red, over x from 0 to 1, with observed points marked as circles and squares. Panel (b), 'Acquisition Landscape', overlays the EHVI curve (solid dark navy) and the REHVI curve (dashed orange). Each has a multi-peaked profile, and vertical dashed lines mark the two argmax locations. EHVI peaks at x of about 0.66 and REHVI at about 0.29. Panel (c), 'Objective Space', plots f1 against f2. A blue Pareto front line with orange X markers for the CAPS-set is drawn, along with red circles for EHVI posterior samples, purple squares for REHVI samples, and a gray triangle for the reference point. Colors stay consistent across panels, so the eye tracks the two maximizers from left to right.
caption: Difference between REHVI and EHVI on a bi-objective problem. (a) The two underlying objective functions and the observed solutions. (b) The acquisition landscapes of REHVI and EHVI, with their respective maximizers. (c) The current CAPS-set and posterior samples of the solutions selected by EHVI and REHVI. The REHVI-selected solution (purple) yields a larger replacement-aware hypervolume gain, despite contributing less to the total hypervolume on its own.
abstract: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) traditionally aims to approximate the entire Pareto front, but, due to resource constraints, real-world deployment is often limited to testing a small, representative subset of solutions. Hence current methods first approximate the full front before selecting solutions, potentially wasting costly evaluations. We formalize this problem as Multi-objective Bayesian Optimization with Cardinality-aware Pareto Selection (MOBO-CAPS), where the goal is to identify a set of exactly M solutions with high hypervolume. We propose two practical cardinality-aware acquisition strategies: REHVI, a replacement-aware approximation to expected hypervolume improvement, and CHO-UCB, which constructs an optimistic M-point set by optimizing a collective UCB-based hypervolume objective. We prove a sublinear simple regret bound for the batched version of CHO-UCB, and empirically show that cardinality-aware acquisition design improves over standard MOBO followed by post-hoc subset selection across nine benchmarks.
